title: Zee Just Secured FIFA World Cup Rights in India With Days to Spare. FIFA Had to Cut Its Price by More Than Half.
excerpt: The deal ends a months-long broadcast standoff that nearly blacked out 1.4 billion people from the world's biggest sporting event — and tells a story about FIFA's fading leverage in cricket-mad India
body:
Ten days. That is how close India came to a total broadcast blackout for the biggest sporting event on the planet.

Zee Entertainment announced on Monday that it has secured the rights to broadcast the 2026 FIFA World Cup and 38 other FIFA events through 2034, ending months of negotiations that had descended into something resembling a standoff. The tournament kicks off on June 11 across the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

## A Price That Tells a Story

Financial terms were not officially disclosed, but the numbers that have leaked tell a story about how FIFA's leverage in India collapsed over the past year. The governing body initially sought around $100 million for the India package covering the 2026 and 2030 World Cups. It eventually slashed its asking price to $60 million. Industry sources suggest the final deal closed somewhere between $25 million and $80 million — a fraction of the original ask.

The gap between aspiration and reality was shaped by a single fact: India does not have a team in the tournament. Without national team participation, FIFA's pricing power in the world's most populated country evaporated.

India's dominant sports broadcaster JioStar — the Reliance-Disney joint venture that aired the 2022 World Cup through its predecessor Viacom18 — offered approximately $20 million. FIFA rejected it. Sony, which held the rights for the 2014 and 2018 tournaments, held discussions but ultimately chose not to bid.

## The Delhi High Court Factor

The standoff had grown serious enough to reach the courts. The Delhi High Court issued notices to the Centre and Prasar Bharati following a petition seeking a mandatory free-to-air broadcast on DD Sports. Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav issued the notice while hearing a writ petition arguing that Indian football fans had a constitutional right not to be blacked out from the world's most-watched sporting event.

The legal pressure likely accelerated the deal. A broadcast blackout in a country of 1.4 billion people — one where 110 million viewers consumed World Cup content digitally during the 2022 tournament in Qatar — would have raised uncomfortable questions for FIFA's global sponsors.

## What Zee Gets

The deal is comprehensive. Beyond the 2026 World Cup, Zee secured the 2030 World Cup, the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup, and a suite of youth tournaments, futsal events, and the FIFA Intercontinental Cup through 2034 — 39 events in total. The matches will be available on Zee's Unite8 Sports channels and its ZEE5 streaming platform.

For Zee, the acquisition is a strategic bet on football's growth trajectory in India. The company has launched four dedicated sports channels — Unite8 Sports 1 and 2, each with HD variants — positioning itself as a challenger to JioStar's dominance in the Indian sports broadcasting market.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the estimated 5.4 million Indian-origin residents across the United States, Canada, and the UK, the FIFA deal carries a practical question: how will they watch? ZEE5's international availability means diaspora viewers may finally have a dedicated Indian-language streaming option for the World Cup — something that could matter during a tournament hosted in North American time zones that are actually convenient for Indian viewers in the West.

The contrast with China is instructive. China's state broadcaster CMG sealed a comprehensive deal with FIFA on May 15 — three weeks before India's deal closed. Beijing negotiated from a position of strategic interest. India's deal came together at the last minute, driven less by strategic vision than by the sheer impracticability of leaving one of the world's largest football audiences without access.

The 2026 World Cup starts in eight days. For Indian fans, the blackout is over. For FIFA, the lesson is that India's cricket-dominated sports market does not automatically translate into premium pricing for football — no matter how large the audience.
author: Diaspora Desk
